title: Composition of Functions
seo_title: Precalculus Composition of Functions Worksheets (TEKS P.2A–P.2C)
standard_text: P.2A use the composition of two functions to model and solve real-world problems; P.2B demonstrate that function composition is not always commutative; P.2C represent a given function as a composite function of two or more functions
meta_desc: Free Precalculus worksheets on composition of functions for Texas TEKS P.2A to P.2C: evaluate and write f(g(x)), order of composition, decomposing functions and real-world composition. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: f(g(x)): do g first, then f.
key_sub: f(g(x)) and g(f(x)) are usually different.
body_html:
How to think about it

  • (f ∘ g)(x) = f(g(x)): do g first, then put the result into f.
  • Composition is not always commutative: f(g(x)) and g(f(x)) are usually different.
  • To decompose h, look for an inner expression. In (2x + 1)3, the inner function is 2x + 1 and the outer function is x3.
  • In real situations, the output of the first step is the input of the second.

Examples

Example

f(x) = 2x + 1, g(x) = x2

f(g(3)) = f(9) = 19

g(f(3)) = g(7) = 49

Answer: 19 ≠ 49

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Working from the outside inStart with the inner function.
Swapping f and gf(g(x)): g is inside.
Assuming the order does not matterCheck both orders: they are usually different.

faq.q: Is there more than one way to decompose a function?
faq.a: Yes. Any pair that gives the same h works; the usual choice uses a clear inner expression.
